danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Fyrst Andrejs øjne fulgte stadig Pfuel ud af værelset, da grev Bennigsen trådte hastigt ind, nikkede til Bolkonskij, men gik uden at standse videre ind i arbejdsværelset og gav instruktioner til sin adjudant undervejs. Kejseren fulgte efter ham, og Bennigsen havde skyndt sig for at gøre forberedelser og være klar til at modtage regenten. Tjernýsjev og fyrst Andrej gik ud på trappen, hvor kejseren, der så træt ud, var ved at stige af hesten. Markis Paulucci talte til ham med særlig varme, og kejseren lyttede med hovedet bøjet til venstre og en utilfreds mine. Kejseren gik fremad, tydeligvis i ønsket om at afslutte samtalen, men den rødmende og ophidsede italiener, der ikke tog hensyn til etiketten, fulgte efter ham og blev ved med at tale.

»Og hvad angår den mand, der foreslog denne lejr — Drissa-lejren,« sagde Paulucci, da kejseren gik op ad trappen og lagde mærke til fyrst Andrej og lod sit blik glide over det ukendte ansigt, »hvad angår den person, sire...« fortsatte Paulucci desperat, tilsyneladende ude af stand til at holde sig tilbage, »den mand, der anbefalede Drissa-lejren — jeg ser intet andet alternativ end galehuset eller galgen!«
Uden at agte på den italienske bemærknings afslutning, og som om han ikke hørte den, genkendte kejseren Bolkonskij og henvendte sig nådigt til ham.
»Jeg er meget glad for at se Dem! Gå derind, hvor de holder møde, og vent på mig.«

Kejseren gik ind i arbejdsværelset. Han blev fulgt af fyrst Pjotr Mikhailovitj Volkónskij og baron Stein, og døren lukkede bag dem. Fyrst Andrej, der benyttede sig af kejserens tilladelse, fulgte med Paulucci, som han kendte fra Tyrkiet, ind i dagligstuen, hvor rådet var samlet.

Fyrst Pjotr Mikhailovitj Volkónskij indtog så at sige stillingen som chef for kejserens stab. Han kom ud af arbejdsværelset ind i dagligstuen med nogle kort, som han bredte ud på et bord, og stillede spørgsmål, som han ønskede de tilstedeværende herrers mening om. Det, der var sket, var, at der i løbet af natten var indløbet nyheder (som senere viste sig at være falske) om en bevægelse fra franskmændenes side for at omgå Drissa-lejren.

Den første, der talte, var general Armfeldt, som for at imødegå den foreliggende vanskelighed uventet foreslog en helt ny position borte fra Petersburg- og Moskva-vejene. Grunden hertil var uforklarlig (medmindre han ønskede at vise, at også han kunne have en mening), men han hævdede, at hæren på dette punkt burde forenes og dér afvente fjenden. Det var tydeligt, at Armfeldt havde udtænkt denne plan for længe siden og nu fremlagde den, ikke så meget for at besvare de stillede spørgsmål — som hans plan faktisk ikke besvarede — men for at benytte lejligheden til at fremføre den. Det var en af de millioner af forslag, alle lige gode, der kunne fremsættes, så længe det var ganske ukendt, hvilken karakter krigen ville få. Nogle bestred hans argumenter, andre forsvarede dem. Den unge grev Toll modsatte sig den svenske generals synspunkter mere heftigt end nogen anden, og under diskussionen trak han fra sin sidelomme en velspækket notesbog, som han bad om tilladelse til at læse op af. I disse omfangsrige notater foreslog Toll en helt anden plan, der afveg fuldstændigt fra Armfeldts og Pfuels. Til svar på Toll foreslog Paulucci en fremrykning og et angreb, som han hævdede var det eneste, der kunne befri os fra den nuværende usikkerhed og fra fælden (som han kaldte Drissa-lejren), hvori vi befandt os.

Under alle disse diskussioner var Pfuel og hans tolk, Wolzogen (hans »bro« i hofrelationerne), tavse. Pfuel nøjedes med foragteligt at fnøse og vende sig bort for at vise, at han aldrig ville nedlade sig til at svare på det nonsens, han nu hørte. Så da fyrst Volkónskij, der sad for bordenden, opfordrede ham til at give sin mening, sagde han blot:

»Hvorfor spørge mig? General Armfeldt har foreslået en pragtfuld position med ubeskyttet ryg, eller hvad med den italienske herres angreb — fortræffeligt, eller et tilbagetog, også godt! Hvorfor spørge mig?« sagde han. »I ved jo selv alt bedre end jeg.«
Men da Volkónskij med rynket pande sagde, at det var i kejserens navn, han bad om hans mening, rejste Pfuel sig, og idet han pludselig blev livlig, begyndte han at tale:

»Alt er blevet ødelagt, alt er bragt i uorden, alle troede, de vidste bedre end jeg, og nu kommer I til mig! Hvordan rette op på det? Der er intet at rette op! De principper, jeg har fastlagt, skal følges nøje,« sagde han og trommede på bordet med sine knoklede fingre. »Hvad er vanskeligheden? Nonsens, barneri!«

Han gik hen til kortet og begyndte i hastig tale at bevise, at ingen uventet hændelse kunne ændre Drissa-lejrens effektivitet, at alt var forudset, og at hvis fjenden virkelig agtede at omgå den, ville fjenden uundgåeligt blive tilintetgjort.

Paulucci, der ikke forstod tysk, begyndte at stille ham spørgsmål på fransk. Wolzogen kom sin chef til hjælp, da denne talte dårligt fransk, og begyndte at oversætte for ham, idet han knap kunne følge med Pfuel, der hastigt demonstrerede, at ikke blot alt, hvad der var sket, men alt, hvad der kunne ske, var forudset i hans plan, og at hvis der nu var vanskeligheder, lå hele skylden i, at hans plan ikke var præcist udført. Han lo sarkastisk, han demonstrerede, og til sidst holdt han foragteligt op med at demonstrere, som en matematiker der holder op med at bevise rigtigheden af et problem, der allerede er bevist, på forskellige måder. Wolzogen overtog hans plads og fortsatte med at forklare sine synspunkter på fransk, idet han af og til vendte sig mod Pfuel og sagde: »Er det ikke sådan, Deres Excellence?« Men Pfuel, som en mand der i kampens hede slår sine egne, råbte vredt ad sin egen støtte, Wolzogen:
»Nå, selvfølgelig, hvad mere er der at forklare?«
Paulucci og Michaud angreb begge Wolzogen samtidig på fransk. Armfeldt henvendte sig til Pfuel på tysk. Toll forklarede Volkónskij på russisk. Fyrst Andrej lyttede og iagttog i tavshed.

Af alle disse mænd sympatiserede fyrst Andrej mest med Pfuel, der var vred, beslutsom og absurd selvsikker. Af alle de tilstedeværende var det tydeligvis kun ham, der ikke søgte noget for sig selv, ikke nærede had til nogen og kun ønskede, at planen, udformet efter en teori opnået ved års slid, skulle gennemføres. Han var latterlig og ubehageligt sarkastisk, men alligevel indgød han uvilkårlig respekt ved sin grænseløse hengivenhed for en idé. Desuden havde alle de andres bemærkninger, undtagen Pfuels, ét fælles træk, der ikke havde været mærkbart ved krigsrådet i 1805: der var nu en panisk frygt for Napoleons geni, som, omend skjult, var mærkbar i hvert eneste modsvar. Alt antog man var muligt for Napoleon, man ventede ham fra alle sider og påkaldte hans frygtelige navn for at knuse hinandens forslag. Pfuel alene syntes at betragte Napoleon som en barbar ligesom alle andre, der modsatte sig hans teori. Men foruden denne respektfølelse vakte Pfuel medlidenhed hos fyrst Andrej. Af den tone, hvori hoffolk tiltalte ham, og af den måde Paulucci havde tilladt sig at tale om ham til kejseren, men frem for alt ud fra en vis fortvivlelse i Pfuels egne udtryk, var det klart, at de andre vidste, og Pfuel selv følte, at hans fald var nært forestående. Og trods sin selvtillid og gnækkende tyske sarkasme var han ynkelig med sit glattede hår ved tindingerne og de totter, der stak op bagpå. Selv om han skjulte det under et skær af irritation og foragt, var han tydeligvis i fortvivlelse over, at den eneste tilbageværende chance for at afprøve sin teori i et kolossalt eksperiment og bevise dens rigtighed for hele verden var ved at glide ham af hænde.

Diskussionerne varede længe, og jo længere de varede, jo mere ophidsede blev stridighederne, kulminerende i råben og personlige angreb, og jo mindre muligt var det at nå nogen samlet konklusion ud fra alt det, der var blevet sagt. Fyrst Andrej, der lyttede til denne mangesprogede tale og disse gisninger, planer, gendrivelser og råb, følte kun forbavselse over, hvad de sagde. En tanke, der længe og ofte var faldet ham ind under hans militære virke — tanken om, at der ikke findes og ikke kan findes nogen krigsvidenskab, og at der derfor ikke kan findes noget sådant som et militært geni — forekom ham nu at være en indlysende sandhed. »Hvilken teori og videnskab er mulig i en sag, hvor betingelserne og omstændighederne er ukendte og ikke kan fastlægges, især da de kæmpende styrkers størrelse ikke kan bestemmes? Ingen var eller er i stand til at forudse, i hvilken tilstand vor eller fjendens hær vil være om en dag, og ingen kan vurdere styrken af denne eller hin afdeling. Undertiden — når der ikke er en kujon forrest, som råber: 'Vi er afskåret!' og begynder at løbe, men en modig og munter fyr, der råber 'Hurra!' — er en afdeling på fem tusind mand tredive tusind værd, som ved Schön Grabern, mens til andre tider halvtreds tusind flygter for otte tusind, som ved Austerlitz. Hvilken videnskab kan der være i en sag, hvor, som i alle praktiske anliggender, intet kan fastlægges, og alt afhænger af utallige betingelser, hvis betydning bestemmes i et bestemt øjeblik, som ingen ved hvornår indtræffer? Armfeldt siger, at vor hær er skåret midt over, og Paulucci siger, vi har den franske hær mellem to ildebrande; Michaud siger, at Drissa-lejrens svaghed ligger i at have floden bag sig, og Pfuel siger, at netop det er dens styrke; Toll foreslår én plan, Armfeldt en anden, og de er alle gode og alle dårlige, og fordelene ved ethvert forslag kan først ses i prøvens stund. Og hvorfor taler de alle om 'militært geni'? Er en mand et geni, som kan beordre brød bragt frem til rette tid og sige, hvem der skal gå til højre og hvem til venstre? Det er kun, fordi militærfolk er omgivet af pomp og magt og skarer af sykofanter smigrer magten og tillægger den geniale egenskaber, den ikke besidder. De bedste generaler, jeg har kendt, var tværtimod dumme eller adspredte mænd. Bagratión var den bedste, Napoleon selv indrømmede det. Og Bonaparte selv! Jeg husker hans indskrænkede, selvtilfredse ansigt på slagmarken ved Austerlitz. Ikke alene behøver en god hærfører ikke nogen særlige egenskaber — tværtimod har han brug for fraværet af de højeste og bedste menneskelige egenskaber: kærlighed, poesi, ømhed og filosofisk søgende tvivl. Han bør være indskrænket, fast overbevist om, at det, han gør, er meget vigtigt (ellers vil han ikke have tilstrækkelig tålmodighed), og kun da vil han være en modig leder. Gud forbyde, at han er human, at han elsker eller ynker eller tænker på, hvad der er retfærdigt og uretfærdigt. Det er forståeligt, at en teori om deres 'geni' for længst blev opfundet for dem, fordi de har magten! Succesen af en militær handling afhænger ikke af dem, men af manden i geleddet, som råber: 'Vi er tabt!' eller som råber: 'Hurra!' Og kun i geleddet kan man tjene med visheden om at være nyttig.«
Således tænkte fyrst Andrej, mens han lyttede til samtalen, og han vågnede først op, da Paulucci kaldte på ham, og alle var ved at gå.

Ved næste dags parade spurgte kejseren fyrst Andrej, hvor han ønskede at gøre tjeneste, og fyrst Andrej mistede for altid sin stilling i hofkredsene ved ikke at bede om at forblive knyttet til regentens person, men om tilladelse til at tjene i hæren.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Prince Andrew's eyes were still following Pfuel out of the room when Count Bennigsen entered hurriedly, and nodding to Bolkonsky but not pausing, went into the study, giving instructions to his adjutant as he went. The Emperor was following him, and Bennigsen had hurried ahead to make some preparations and be ready to receive the sovereign. Chernyshev and Prince Andrew went out onto the porch, where the Emperor, who looked fatigued, was dismounting. Marquis Paulucci was talking to him with particular intensity, and the Emperor, with his head tilted to the left, was listening with a displeased expression. The Emperor moved forward, clearly wanting to end the conversation, but the flushed and excited Italian, ignoring etiquette, followed him and kept talking.

"And as for the man who advised building this camp — the Drissa camp," said Paulucci, as the Emperor mounted the steps and noticed Prince Andrew's unfamiliar face, "as to that person, sire..." continued Paulucci desperately, apparently unable to stop himself, "the man who advised the Drissa camp — I see no alternative but the madhouse or the gallows!"
Without paying attention to the end of the Italian's remarks, and as though not hearing them, the Emperor recognized Bolkonsky and addressed him warmly.
"I'm very glad to see you! Go in where they are meeting, and wait for me."

The Emperor went into the study. He was followed by Prince Peter Mikhaylovich Volkonsky and Baron Stein, and the door closed behind them. Prince Andrew, taking advantage of the Emperor's permission, accompanied Paulucci — whom he had known in Turkey — into the drawing room where the council was assembled.

Prince Peter Mikhaylovich Volkonsky occupied the position of, as it were, chief of the Emperor's staff. He came out of the study into the drawing room with some maps which he spread on a table, and put questions on which he wished to hear the opinions of those present. What had happened was that news (which later proved false) had been received during the night of a French movement to outflank the Drissa camp.

The first to speak was General Armfeldt, who to address the difficulty unexpectedly proposed an entirely new position away from the Petersburg and Moscow roads. The reason for this was inexplicable (unless he wanted to show that he too could have an opinion), but he urged that the army should unite at this point and there await the enemy. It was clear that Armfeldt had thought out this plan long ago and now presented it not so much to answer the questions posed — which in fact his plan did not answer — but to seize the opportunity to air it. It was one of the millions of proposals, one as good as another, that could be made as long as it was completely unknown what form the war would take. Some disputed his arguments, others supported them. Young Count Toll objected to the Swedish general's views more heatedly than anyone else, and in the course of the argument drew from his pocket a well-filled notebook, which he asked permission to read. In these voluminous notes Toll suggested an entirely different scheme from either Armfeldt's or Pfuel's plan. In response to Toll, Paulucci proposed an advance and an attack, which he said was the only way to escape the present uncertainty and the trap (as he called the Drissa camp) in which they were stuck.

Throughout all these discussions, Pfuel and his interpreter Wolzogen (his "bridge" in court relations) remained silent. Pfuel merely snorted contemptuously and turned away, making it clear he would never lower himself to respond to the nonsense he was hearing. So when Prince Volkonsky, who was chairing the meeting, called on him for his opinion, he simply said:

"Why ask me? General Armfeldt has proposed a splendid position with an exposed rear, or why not this Italian gentleman's plan of attack — very fine! Or a retreat — also good! Why ask me?" he said. "After all, you yourselves know everything better than I do."
But when Volkonsky said with a frown that he was asking in the Emperor's name, Pfuel rose and, suddenly animated, began to speak:

"Everything has been ruined, everything muddled! Everyone thought they knew better than I did, and now you come to me! How can it be fixed? There is nothing to fix! The principles I laid down must be followed strictly," he said, drumming on the table with his bony fingers. "What is the difficulty? Nonsense! Childishness!"

He strode to the map and, speaking rapidly, began demonstrating that no eventuality could undermine the effectiveness of the Drissa camp, that everything had been foreseen, and that if the enemy were truly going to outflank it, they would inevitably be destroyed.

Paulucci, who did not know German, began questioning him in French. Wolzogen came to his chief's aid — Pfuel spoke French badly — and began translating for him, barely able to keep pace as Pfuel rapidly demonstrated that not only everything that had happened, but everything that could possibly happen, had been foreseen in his plan, and that if difficulties had arisen, the entire fault lay in the fact that his plan had not been executed precisely. He laughed sarcastically, he proved his points, and finally ceased his demonstration with contempt, like a mathematician who stops bothering to prove a problem he considers already proven. Wolzogen took over and continued explaining in French, turning every now and then to Pfuel: "Is that not so, Your Excellency?" But Pfuel, like a man in a fight who lashes out at his own allies, shouted angrily at his own supporter Wolzogen:
"Well, of course — what more is there to explain?"
Paulucci and Michaud attacked Wolzogen simultaneously in French. Armfeldt addressed Pfuel in German. Toll explained things to Volkonsky in Russian. Prince Andrew listened and observed in silence.

Of all these men, Prince Andrew felt the most sympathy for Pfuel — angry, determined, and absurdly self-confident though he was. Of everyone present, he alone was clearly not seeking anything for himself, harbored no hatred toward anyone, and simply wanted the plan he had developed through years of work to be carried out. He was ridiculous and unpleasantly sarcastic, yet he inspired involuntary respect through his boundless devotion to an idea. Besides this, the remarks of all the others except Pfuel shared one trait that had not been noticeable at the council of war in 1805: there was now a barely concealed panic fear of Napoleon's genius, evident in every rejoinder. Everything was assumed to be possible for Napoleon; they expected him from every direction and invoked his terrible name to demolish each other's proposals. Pfuel alone seemed to regard Napoleon as a barbarian, no different from anyone else who opposed his theory. But beyond respect, Pfuel also stirred pity in Prince Andrew. From the tone in which the courtiers addressed him, from the way Paulucci had spoken of him to the Emperor, and above all from a certain desperation in Pfuel's own manner, it was clear that the others knew — and Pfuel himself sensed — that his downfall was at hand. And despite his self-assurance and his gruff German sarcasm, he was pitiable, with his hair neatly smoothed at the temples and sticking up in tufts at the back. Though he hid it behind a show of irritation and contempt, he was plainly in despair that the sole remaining chance to test his theory through a great experiment and prove its soundness to the whole world was slipping away from him.

The discussions dragged on, and the longer they lasted, the more heated the disputes became — culminating in shouts and personal attacks — and the less possible it was to reach any general conclusion. Prince Andrew, listening to this babel of languages and to these conjectures, plans, refutations, and outbursts, felt nothing but amazement at what they were all saying. A thought that had long since and often occurred to him during his military service — the idea that there is not and cannot be any science of war, and that therefore there can be no such thing as military genius — now struck him as an obvious truth. "What theory and science can apply to a matter whose conditions and circumstances are unknown and cannot be defined, especially when the strength of the forces involved cannot be measured? No one was or is able to foresee what position our army or the enemy's will be in tomorrow, and no one can gauge the real strength of any given detachment. Sometimes — when there is no coward at the front to shout 'We're cut off!' and start running, but instead a brave and cheerful fellow who shouts 'Hurrah!' — a force of five thousand is worth thirty thousand, as at Schön Grabern, while at other times fifty thousand flee from eight thousand, as at Austerlitz. What science can govern a matter in which, as in all practical affairs, nothing can be precisely determined and everything depends on countless conditions whose significance reveals itself only at a particular moment that no one can predict? Armfeldt says our army is cut in half, and Paulucci says we have the French between two fires; Michaud says the Drissa camp is worthless because the river is behind it, while Pfuel says that is exactly what makes it strong; Toll proposes one plan, Armfeldt another — and they are all good and all bad, because the merits of any proposal can only be seen at the moment of execution. And why do they all talk of 'military genius'? Is a man a genius because he can order bread to be brought up at the right time and tell soldiers to go right or left? It is only because military leaders are surrounded by pomp, power, and crowds of sycophants who flatter authority by attributing to it qualities of genius it does not possess. The best generals I have known were, on the contrary, stupid or absent-minded men. Bagration (Pyotr Bagration) was the best — Napoleon himself admitted it. And Napoleon himself! I remember his smug, self-satisfied face on the field of Austerlitz. Not only does a good commander not need any special qualities — on the contrary, he needs the absence of the highest and best human attributes: love, poetry, tenderness, and philosophic, questioning doubt. He should be narrow-minded, firmly convinced that what he is doing is enormously important (otherwise he will lack the necessary patience), and only then will he be a brave leader. God forbid that he should be humane, that he should love or feel pity, or think about what is just and unjust. It is no wonder that a theory of their 'genius' was invented for them long ago, because they hold power! The success of a military action depends not on them but on the man in the ranks who shouts 'We're lost!' or who shouts 'Hurrah!' And only in the ranks can one serve with the assurance of being truly useful."
So thought Prince Andrew as he listened to the debate, and he roused himself only when Paulucci called to him and everyone began to leave.

At the review the next day, the Emperor asked Prince Andrew where he would like to serve, and Prince Andrew lost his standing in court circles forever by not asking to remain attached to the sovereign's person, but requesting permission to serve with the army.
